analysis.one_liner: Banned surprise credit card rate hikes, penalty fees, and card marketing to people under 21.
analysis.headline: Senator Dodd's credit card reform bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced in March 2005 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced credit card companies to give 15 days' notice before raising your interest rate and let you cancel the card and pay off the balance at the old rate. It would have banned charging interest on amounts paid on time, punishing people for paying in full, and charging over-limit fees on transactions the company itself approved. It would have required statements to show how long — and at what total cost — paying only the minimum would take, restricted issuing cards to anyone under 21 without a cosigner, income, or approved counseling, and let bankruptcy courts discharge debt charged at rates more than 20 points above prime.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that carry credit card balances. The bill targeted the practices card issuers used to raise rates on existing balances, charge fees for prompt payment, and enroll students in high-fee cards. Borrowers who fell into debt at very high rates would have gained a path to discharge that debt in bankruptcy.

how_it_helps.text: Credit card companies would have to give at least 15 days' notice before raising an interest rate, and could not apply the new rate to the balance you already owe; you could cancel and pay off the old balance at the old rate.
Card issuers could not charge finance or interest charges on new credit that was paid on time, and could not impose fees or penalties for paying a balance in full or paying more than the minimum.
Card issuers could not charge over-the-limit fees on transactions the creditor itself approved.
Monthly statements would have to show how many months it would take to pay off the balance paying only the minimum, the total cost of doing so, and the payment needed to be debt-free in three years.
Solicitations offering low introductory 'teaser' rates would have to clearly disclose the rate that applies afterward and any conditions that could void the teaser rate.

No credit card could be issued to anyone under 21 without a cosigner, proof of independent ability to repay, or completion of an approved nonprofit credit counseling course, and colleges' affinity card agreements could not bypass these rules.

In bankruptcy, credit card debt charged at an annual rate more than 20 percentage points above the prime rate would not be protected from discharge, giving debtors a legal remedy against extreme rates.
Penalties for violating these disclosure rules on credit card accounts would be doubled, with higher penalties for a pattern of violations.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies that profit from penalty interest rates, over-limit fees, and late-fee traps — would bear the cost of giving up those revenue streams. Borrowers who currently cross-subsidize low rates for prompt payers could face higher rates or tighter credit standards.

drawbacks.text: Restricting cards for people under 21 could have blocked young adults without a cosigner, income, or completed counseling from building credit on their own, a trade-off supporters of the bill accepted to stop student debt traps.

Making very-high-rate credit card debt easier to discharge in bankruptcy shifts those losses to creditors and, indirectly, could raise rates for other borrowers — the standard objection the banking industry would raise to Title III.
Much of the bill relies on disclosure: monthly statements and mailings become more informative, but only help consumers who read them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — notice before rate hikes, no penalties for paying on time, honest payoff math on the statement — directly target practices that pushed cardholders deeper into debt, and the costs fall mainly on the issuers earning those fees. The under-21 restrictions and the bankruptcy provision involve real trade-offs in credit availability and creditor losses, but they are narrow and paired with disclosure and counseling requirements rather than outright bans. On balance this was a fairly designed consumer protection bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd introduced the Credit Card Act of 2005 in the Senate on March 2, 2005.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the committee with jurisdiction over consumer credit law.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further steps of any kind after the referral, through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept the ability to raise rates on existing balances, charge fees for on-time and full payments, and market cards to students until a substantially similar Credit Card Act passed and was signed in 2009 — meaning cardholders paid several more years of these charges while this bill sat untouched.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Republican in the Republican-controlled 109th Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 2, 2005 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Credit card issuers and their trade associations
against.role: Banks and card companies whose penalty rates and fees the bill restricted
against.what_they_did: Opposed credit card regulation of this kind through lobbying during this era; the bill drew no Republican support and never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Senate Banking Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and card companies)
industries.note: The bill removes several of the industry's main penalty revenue streams: rate increases applied retroactively to existing balances, interest charged on amounts paid on time, fees for paying in full, over-limit fees on approved transactions, and easy card issuance to students. Its interest runs against cardholders in this bill, since the revenue comes from charges to borrowers.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities with affinity card agreements
industries.note: The bill bars issuing cards to students under 21 through campus affinity card agreements without meeting the adult-application requirements, limiting a marketing channel card issuers paid schools to access.

Underage applicants could qualify for a card by completing counseling at a Board-approved nonprofit agency, creating a funded role for compliant agencies and standards that exclude agencies whose boards or counselors profit from outcomes.
